source.title: Mental Efficiency, and Other Hints to Men and Women
source.attribution: Arnold Bennett, Mental Efficiency, and Other Hints to Men and Women, Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: 1911 George H. Doran edition (Gutenberg #23347; the brief's #2846 is a different ebook). Arnold Bennett died in 1931, so the work is public domain worldwide. Text fetched from the GITenberg mirror.

cards.title: Your mind gets out of shape just like your body
cards.body:
Bennett noticed that people happily spend a quarter of an hour a day on physical exercises, yet never think of training their minds. After months of light reading and news, he says, most of us would find a hard subject leaves us puffing within minutes, and we simply give up.

His point is that mental slackness is not a fixed trait. Like an unfit body, an unfit mind is mostly the result of neglect, and it responds to regular, deliberate exercise. The first step is to notice the condition honestly instead of quietly accepting it.
cards.quote: The average mind is vastly more complicated, not less sadly out of order, but perhaps even more susceptible to culture.
cards.apply_it: Try reading something genuinely demanding for 15 minutes today. Notice when you want to quit, and keep going two minutes past that point.

quiz.question: What does Bennett compare an untrained mind to?
options: A body that has gone unfit through neglect
A machine that can never be repaired
A library with too many books
A garden that grows best when left alone
quiz.explanation: He argues the mind, like the body, falls out of condition through neglect and can be trained back.

cards.title: The hard part isn't starting, it's continuing
cards.body:
Bennett asked why so many people who long to learn never actually do. His answer: it is not a lack of desire, and not even a lack of will to begin. Most of us can start. What fails us is the will to keep going once the first enthusiasm fades.

This reframes the problem. If you keep abandoning plans, the fix isn't a more exciting start. It's designing for the dull middle: a routine small enough to survive bad weeks, and a way to restart quickly after a lapse.
cards.quote: It is not the absence of desire that prevents them. It is, first, the absence of will-power--not the will to begin, but the will to continue
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you dropped. Write down the exact week it faded and what got in the way then.

quiz.question: According to Bennett, what kind of will-power do most people lack?
options: The will to begin something new
The will to continue after starting
The will to resist temptation
The will to compete with others
quiz.explanation: He says people can start; it's continuing that fails them.

cards.title: Poor concentration is a sign your mind needs training
cards.body:
When Bennett's readers wrote in about their mental slackness, one letter blamed it on a lack of concentration. Bennett agreed: an inability to fix the mind on one thing is one of the clearest signs that it is out of condition.

Today, with constant notifications, scattered attention can feel normal. Bennett's framing helps: wandering focus is not a character flaw to feel guilty about, but a symptom that improves with practice, just as breathlessness improves with regular walking.
cards.quote: I thoroughly agree that inability to concentrate is one of the chief symptoms of the mental machine being out of condition.
cards.apply_it: Set a timer for 10 minutes and work on one task with your phone in another room. Count how often your mind wanders.

quiz.question: How does Bennett treat an inability to concentrate?
options: As an inborn flaw that can't change
As unimportant compared to memory
As a symptom of a mind out of condition
As a problem only for women
quiz.explanation: He sees poor concentration as a key symptom of an untrained mind, one that can improve.

cards.title: Deciding is easy; following through for months is the real test
cards.body:
A reader sent Bennett a hopeful verse claiming that tasks chosen in a bright moment can be completed through dark ones. Bennett disagreed. Making a resolution, he says, takes only a moment of inspiration, often borrowed from someone more energetic. Carrying it out day after day for months or years is the genuinely hard thing.

Knowing this protects you from overconfidence. A burst of motivation is not evidence that you will finish; it's only the cheapest part of the process. Plan for the gloomy days, because they will come.
cards.quote: To will is easy: it needs but the momentary bright contagion of a stronger spirit than one's own.
cards.apply_it: For your current goal, write down what you will do on a day when you feel no motivation at all.

quiz.question: What does Bennett say is the hard part of a resolution?
options: Choosing the right goal
Finding inspiration
Telling others about it
Fulfilling it day after day over months
quiz.explanation: He says willing takes a moment; fulfilling it through gloomy months is the real difficulty.

cards.title: The method matters less than the spirit you bring to it
cards.body:
Many of Bennett's readers hoped a memory course or mind-training system would fix their mental slackness. Bennett was sceptical. Such systems might help or might not, he said, but no class can remake a person. Even the best method depends entirely on your own resolve.

The same is true of today's apps, courses and productivity frameworks. Shopping for the perfect system can become a way of avoiding the work. Pick something reasonable, then focus on how steadily and honestly you use it.
cards.quote: And what really counts is not the system, but the spirit in which the man handles it.
cards.apply_it: If you're comparing methods or apps for a goal, pick one today and commit to it for 30 days.

quiz.question: According to Bennett, what decides whether a mind-training system works?
options: The spirit and resolve of the person using it
How expensive the course is
How famous its author is
How many techniques it contains
quiz.explanation: He says the best system depends utterly on the person's power of resolution.

cards.title: Before a new resolution, plan for the ways you failed before
cards.body:
Bennett pictures a thirty-year-old leaping up, fired with the idea of improving their mind. Sit back down, he says. You've had these moments before and you've failed before, and your will is probably no stronger now. What precautions will you take this time?

He goes on to name the usual causes of failure: taking on too much, being put off by friends' mockery, and not making room in the day. The lesson is to learn from past attempts instead of hoping enthusiasm will carry you further this time.
cards.quote: What precautions are you going to take against failure this time?
cards.apply_it: List the last two goals you abandoned and the main reason each one stalled. Add one safeguard against each to your new plan.

quiz.question: What does Bennett ask people to do before starting a new resolution?
options: Announce it to friends
Think about why past attempts failed and take precautions
Buy a good course
Wait until they feel strongly motivated
quiz.explanation: He asks what precautions you'll take, since your will is probably no stronger than before.

cards.title: Pick a first goal you can't fail, because failure wounds your resolve
cards.body:
Bennett warns that nothing damages the spirit of resolve like a past failure. You think the wound has healed, but at a critical moment it can reopen. So his first rule is: don't start with a grand programme. Choose something almost embarrassingly easy, such as reading one short book twice in a month and making notes.

When it's done, you have the quiet pride of having resolved something and done it. That success gives your mind tone and earns you the right to set a bigger goal next.
cards.quote: And no wound is more cruel to the spirit of resolve than that dealt by failure.
cards.apply_it: Set a one-month goal so easy you're slightly embarrassed by it. Finish it before planning anything bigger.

quiz.question: Why does Bennett advise starting with a very easy goal?
options: Easy goals are all most people can manage
Hard goals are a waste of time
Avoiding an early failure protects your resolve
It impresses your friends
quiz.explanation: Failure wounds resolve, so an easy first success builds confidence for bigger goals.

cards.title: Learn great writing by heart to build concentration
cards.body:
Bennett noticed that musicians practise finger exercises without embarrassment, yet adults feel silly doing mental drills. He thought this false shame was a real obstacle. One of the best drills, he says, is memorising great poetry or prose: about twenty lines a week for six months.

The value isn't the memorised lines themselves. Memorising forces the mind to hold still on one thing, and the ability to concentrate at will is, in his view, the foundation of all self-development.
cards.quote: Yet there are few mental exercises better than learning great poetry or prose by heart.
cards.apply_it: Choose a short poem, proverb or passage you admire and memorise five lines of it this week.

quiz.question: What does Bennett say is the chief benefit of learning poetry by heart?
options: Impressing people at dinner
Improving your handwriting
Learning about history
It forces the mind to concentrate
quiz.explanation: He values memorising mainly because it trains the faculty of concentrating at will.

cards.title: After reading a page, write down everything you remember
cards.body:
Bennett recommends a simple exercise: read a page of anything, then immediately write down all you can recall of it, in your own words or the author's. Fifteen minutes a day, he says, is enough, and the effect surprised him.

The drill turns passive reading into active recall. You quickly discover how much slid past you, and the effort of reconstructing it trains both attention and memory. It is a close cousin of what modern learning research calls retrieval practice.
cards.quote: Another excellent exercise is to read a page of no-matter-what, and then immediately to write down--in one's own words or in the author's--one's full recollection of it.
cards.apply_it: Read one page of a book now, close it, and write down everything you can remember. Then check what you missed.

quiz.question: What is Bennett's 'read a page' exercise?
options: Read a page, then write down all you recall of it
Read a page aloud three times
Read a page and underline key words
Read the last page first
quiz.explanation: He suggests reading a page and immediately writing out your full recollection of it.

cards.title: Keep a journal of what you notice, not just a diary of yourself
cards.body:
Bennett, a professional writer who claimed to hate writing, still insisted that regular writing is essential to mental growth. But he preferred a journal to a diary. A diary records your own doings and tends toward self-absorption. A journal looks outward: the people you met, what they said, what struck you about the world.

He knew a man who kept a journal of every superstition he came across and ended up with a document of real interest. Writing about what you observe sharpens your attention to life itself.
cards.quote: A diary treats exclusively of one's self and one's doings; a journal roams wider, and notes whatever one has observed of interest.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write five sentences about something or someone interesting you observed today, not about yourself.

quiz.question: How does Bennett distinguish a journal from a diary?
options: A journal is private; a diary is public
A journal records what you observe in the world; a diary is mostly about yourself
A diary is longer than a journal
There is no real difference
quiz.explanation: He says a diary is about one's self, while a journal roams wider and notes what one observes.

cards.title: Treat lapses in focus with calm indifference, then carry on
cards.body:
Bennett quotes a reader, an Oxford lecturer, who recommended spending about ten minutes every day concentrating on the highest thoughts one can manage, with absolute regularity. Lapses will be frequent, the lecturer warned, but they should be met with simple indifference and stubborn persistence.

Bennett agreed, though he saw it as an advanced exercise for after the basics. The attitude is useful for any focus practice: wandering attention is expected, and scolding yourself only adds noise. Notice, return, continue.
cards.quote: Failures will be frequent, but they must be regarded with simple indifference and dogged perseverance in the path chosen.
cards.apply_it: During your next focused session, each time your mind wanders, say 'back' silently and return without judging yourself.

quiz.question: How should you respond to frequent failures in daily concentration practice, according to the letter Bennett quotes?
options: Stop the practice until you're ready
Double the session length
Meet them with indifference and keep going
Switch to a different practice
quiz.explanation: The advice is simple indifference to failures and dogged perseverance.

cards.title: You can't fake the impression you leave for long
cards.body:
Bennett observes that we have no real picture of how we come across. And trying hard to make a good impression mostly earns you a reputation as someone who tries hard to make a good impression. In a single interview you might manage how you're seen, but over time people form their view unconsciously, and it reflects who you actually are.

The practical upshot: rather than managing appearances, put your energy into being the kind of person you'd want others to see, because that is what they'll eventually see anyway.
cards.quote: The real impress is, in the end, given unconsciously, not consciously; and further, it is received unconsciously, not consciously.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: in what situation do I try hardest to impress? What would it look like to simply be straightforward there?

quiz.question: What does Bennett say happens when someone tries hard to make a good impression?
options: People see them as someone trying to make a good impression
It always works over time
People ignore it completely
It makes them more likeable
quiz.explanation: He notes the result is that friends set him down as a man who tries to make a good impression.

cards.title: Your most annoying habits are the ones you can't see
cards.body:
Bennett points out that friends judge us with few illusions, just as we quietly note their faults. And the traits in us that irritate others most are usually the ones we're completely unaware of. Looking back ten years, most of us wince at how we must have come across, despite our good intentions.

His question stings: if you see your past self so clearly now, what will you think of your present self in ten years? The reflection builds humility and a healthy reluctance to tread on other people's toes.
cards.quote: Above all it is advisable to comprehend thoroughly that the things in your individuality which annoy your friends most are the things of which you are completely unconscious.
cards.apply_it: Ask one trusted friend: 'What's one habit of mine that might annoy people without me noticing?' Listen without defending.

quiz.question: According to Bennett, which of your traits annoy friends most?
options: The ones you are proud of
The ones you are unaware of
The ones you try to hide
The ones you share with them
quiz.explanation: He says the things that annoy friends most are those of which you're completely unconscious.

cards.title: In friendship, a kind heart matters more than brilliance
cards.body:
Bennett says the final test we apply to friends is a simple one: is this a decent person? Clever, witty or impressive qualities are pleasant, but we return to plain kindliness with relief. It is, he argues, the one quality we cannot do without in a friend.

That's worth remembering when choosing whom to spend time with, and when thinking about what kind of friend you are. Being kind may win less attention than being brilliant, but it is what keeps friendships alive.
cards.quote: Kindliness of heart is not the greatest of human qualities--and its general effect on the progress of the world is not entirely beneficent--but it is the greatest of human qualities in friendship.
cards.apply_it: Think of the friend you trust most. Write down one kind act of theirs you remember, then do something similar for someone this week.

quiz.question: What quality does Bennett call the greatest in friendship?
options: Intelligence
Wit
Kindliness of heart
Loyalty to tradition
quiz.explanation: He calls kindliness of heart the greatest and least dispensable quality in friendship.

cards.title: Making a resolution earns no credit; keeping it does
cards.body:
Writing about New Year's Day, Bennett teases people who sneer at resolutions while secretly making them. Most of us, he says, wake that morning with a cheerful glow of virtue, as though deciding to change were already an achievement.

But the good feeling is borrowed. Only keeping a resolution justifies feeling virtuous about it. It's a useful check against the pleasant buzz of planning, announcing and buying equipment, all of which can feel like progress while nothing has actually changed.
cards.quote: it is not the making of Resolutions, but the keeping of them, which renders pardonable the consciousness of virtue.
cards.apply_it: Look at a recent plan you felt good about making. What is one action you've actually taken on it? If none, do one today.

quiz.question: When, according to Bennett, is it fair to feel virtuous about a resolution?
options: When you write it down
When you tell people about it
When you make it on New Year's Day
When you actually keep it
quiz.explanation: He says it is the keeping of resolutions, not the making, that justifies that feeling.

cards.title: You can't climb forward while tied to the past
cards.body:
Bennett describes people who tie themselves with an unbreakable rope to a post at the bottom of a hill and then struggle to climb. The past, he says, cannot be changed or worked with, and excessive attention to it drains cheerfulness, which he calls a precious attainment.

He argues that the most important resolution is to break with the past. That doesn't mean forgetting lessons; it means refusing to let old habits, old failures or old identities decide what you do today.
cards.quote: a man cannot go forward and stand still at the same time.
cards.apply_it: Name one thing from your past you keep replaying. Write the lesson in one sentence, then decide one forward step for this week.

quiz.question: What image does Bennett use for people held back by the past?
options: Someone tied to a post at the bottom of a hill trying to climb
A ship without a sail
A runner with no finish line
A tree with shallow roots
quiz.explanation: He pictures people tying themselves to an immovable post and then struggling to climb the hill.

cards.title: Treat yesterday as an experiment, not a rule
cards.body:
Bennett suggests an exercise of imagination: look at your life as if you had been born an experienced adult and yesterday was your first day. You would judge yesterday as a trial, question each thing you did, and plan tomorrow with healthy disrespect for it.

Too often we repeat things simply because we did them once, or never try things because we never have. Bennett even suggests most of us should drop half our old vows. Seeing the past as an experiment frees you to keep what works and change what doesn't.
cards.quote: The past is never more than an experiment.
cards.apply_it: Review yesterday as if it were a trial run. Pick one thing to keep and one thing to change tomorrow.

quiz.question: What does Bennett suggest we do with our routines from the past?
options: Keep them because they're proven
Treat them as experiments to question
Abandon all of them at once
Ask others to judge them
quiz.explanation: He says the past is only an experiment, so we should challenge each act with fresh eyes.

cards.title: Take stock of your life before it's too late
cards.body:
Nearing forty, Bennett found himself asking the big questions: what have I got out of life, what am I likely to get, what is it worth? Strangely, he notes, few people ask these in time. Many ask too late, and some never ask at all.

He compares them to shopkeepers who never count their stock or the till, vaguely unhappy with their back room but never fixing it, until it's too late for even a few cushions. A regular, honest review lets you make small improvements while they still matter.
cards.quote: that so few people put the question to themselves in time, that so many put it too late, or even die without putting it.
cards.apply_it: Block 30 minutes this month to ask: what am I getting from my life now, and what one change would improve it?

quiz.question: What does Bennett compare people who never review their lives to?
options: Sailors without a map
Students who skip exams
Shopkeepers who never take stock or count the till
Farmers who forget to plant
quiz.explanation: His image is of shopkeepers who never take stock and only discover the problem too late.

cards.title: Prepare for the future, but don't forget to live now
cards.body:
Bennett imagines preaching a sermon to a crowd: life is a balance between hoping to live one day and living here and now. For most people, he says, the first instinct has the second by the throat. They keep postponing life until after the next promotion, house or milestone.

His advice is not to give up hopes and ambitions, which he calls agreeable deceptions. It's to stop letting them cheat you too much. The life you're living now is as real as any you'll live twenty years from now.
cards.quote: Prepare to live by all means, but for heaven's sake do not forget to live.
cards.apply_it: Name one thing you're postponing 'until things settle down'. Do a small version of it this week.

quiz.question: According to Bennett, what is the common mistake about hope and the present?
options: People don't plan enough for the future
People have no ambitions
People live too much in the past
Hoping to live one day crowds out living now
quiz.explanation: He says the instinct to live someday is throttling the instinct to live here and now.

cards.title: Picture a marriage five or ten years in, not just the honeymoon
cards.body:
Bennett compares two approaches to marriage in his day: the English way of following romance, and the French way of careful, practical arrangement. He gives the French side its best argument: romantic couples fix their eyes on the honeymoon, while a wise choice considers what the marriage will be like five or ten years on.

Bennett himself still favoured love matches. But the question is worth borrowing whatever your culture: beyond attraction, how will this partnership work in ordinary years, with money, family and routine?
cards.quote: When you agree to a marriage you fix your eyes on the honeymoon. When we agree to a marriage we try to see it as it will be five or ten years hence.
cards.apply_it: If you're in a serious relationship, talk together about what an ordinary Tuesday might look like in ten years.

quiz.question: What point does Bennett let the French side make about marriage?
options: Think about how the marriage will be years from now, not just at the start
Love always lasts forever
Marriage is only about money
Never marry for romance
quiz.explanation: The French argument is to see a marriage as it will be five or ten years later, not just the honeymoon.

cards.title: Companionship is the reward marriage reliably gives
cards.body:
After listing honestly all the risks of marriage, from fading passion to troubles with children, Bennett still concludes that the brave choice is to take the adventure. What marriage gives, he says, is a shared life with another person that stays interesting no matter what.

He describes a couple at a sale, completely absorbed in a lively argument, the world forgotten. Even in hard years, he suggests, the interest of a shared life rarely dies. His friend, a bachelor of forty-six, put it simply: anything is better than the void.
cards.quote: The chief reward of marriage is something which marriage is bound to give--companionship whose mysterious interestingness nothing can stale.
cards.apply_it: If you're married or partnered, name one thing about your partner that still surprises or interests you, and tell them.

quiz.question: What does Bennett see as the chief reward of marriage?
options: Financial security
A companionship whose interest never goes stale
Social status
Freedom from loneliness in old age guaranteed
quiz.explanation: He names companionship with an interest nothing can stale; he notes marriage can't guarantee against a lonely old age.

cards.title: Buy a good book you want, even if you won't read it yet
cards.body:
Bennett had hundreds of unread books and saw no shame in it. Critics fret that people buy classics without reading them. He disagreed: there's no 'ought' about reading everything, and the mass of good literature is far too large for anyone with ordinary leisure.

His rule for buying was simple: is it a good book, and do you want it? The chance of reading it soon shouldn't decide. Books on the shelf invite curiosity, and the person who chooses serious books tends, over time, to get something from them.
cards.quote: In buying a book, be influenced by two considerations only. Are you reasonably sure that it is a good book? Have you a desire to possess it?
cards.apply_it: Choose one book you've wanted for a while and get it, from a shop, library or second-hand stall. No pressure to finish it this month.

quiz.question: What two questions does Bennett use when deciding to buy a book?
options: Is it cheap, and is it short?
Is it popular, and will I finish it soon?
Is it good, and do I want it?
Did a critic recommend it, and is it a classic?
quiz.explanation: He says only two things matter: whether it is a good book and whether you want it.

cards.title: You don't have to finish a book you don't enjoy
cards.body:
Bennett says plenty of nonsense is talked about reading as a duty. He read in his limited spare time, for pleasure rather than self-improvement, and felt no obligation to finish books that didn't hold him. Sometimes one book took him a month.

This is freeing advice. Forcing yourself through a book you dislike can turn reading into a chore and make you read less overall. Putting it down and picking up something you actually want to read keeps the habit alive.
cards.quote: I read what I feel inclined to read, and I am conscious of no duty to finish a book that I don't care to finish.
cards.apply_it: If a book has been sitting half-read for weeks because you dread it, give yourself permission to set it aside and start something you're excited about.

quiz.question: What was Bennett's attitude to finishing books?
options: You must always finish what you start
Only finish books by famous authors
Read the ending first
He felt no duty to finish books he didn't care to finish
quiz.explanation: He read for pleasure and felt no obligation to finish a book that didn't interest him.

cards.title: Be wary of success advice from successful people
cards.body:
Bennett argues that successful people are often the worst guides to success. They rarely understand why they succeeded, forget much of their own story, and, when asked to inspire the young, tell the tidy tale that's expected of them.

It is easy, he notes, to explain a finished success in a neat, agreeable way. Modern researchers call a related trap survivorship bias. When you read a success story, ask what was left out: luck, timing, help from others, and the many people who did the same things and didn't succeed.
cards.quote: No one is a worse guide to success than your typical successful man.
cards.apply_it: Next time you read a success story, list two factors the person didn't mention, such as luck, timing, family support or contacts.

quiz.question: Why does Bennett distrust successful people's accounts of their success?
options: They rarely understand their own success and tell the expected story
They are always lying deliberately
They never write about it
They only talk about luck
quiz.explanation: He says they seldom understand the reasons for their own success and tell a conventional, tidy version.

cards.title: Some success is simply luck, so judge people and yourself fairly
cards.body:
Bennett sorts success into types, and the first is pure chance. Imagine betting on red at a casino and winning six, twelve, eighteen times in a row: people would credit you with mysterious powers, though luck alone did it. In life, where winners have reason to hide luck's role, the halo is even easier to grow.

Recognising luck cuts both ways. It keeps you humble when things go well, makes you slower to worship the rich and famous, and stops you from blaming yourself entirely when good effort doesn't pay off.
cards.quote: Nevertheless, there can be no doubt in the minds of persons who have viewed success at close quarters that a proportion of it is due solely and utterly to chance.
cards.apply_it: Think of one success of yours. Write down one way luck or other people helped it happen.

quiz.question: What does Bennett's casino example show?
options: Gambling is a good strategy
People credit lucky winners with powers they don't have
Red always wins eventually
Skill matters more than chance
quiz.explanation: He shows how people wrongly attribute special gifts to someone who simply got lucky.

cards.title: Stay on the lookout for opportunities, like a sailor on a raft
cards.body:
Among people with a talent for success, Bennett noticed one constant: they are always watching for openings. This isn't the same as being industrious. He pictures a castaway on a raft with his shirt as a signal flag. He doesn't work hard all day, but he never stops scanning the horizon, and when a sail appears he waves with total determination.

Alertness can matter as much as effort. Keep an eye out for chances in your field, and when one shows up, act on it fully.
cards.quote: The man with the talent to succeed is the man on the raft who never goes to sleep.
cards.apply_it: Spend 15 minutes this week scanning for openings in your field: job posts, events, people to contact. Act on one.

quiz.question: In Bennett's raft image, what marks the person likely to succeed?
options: Rowing hard all day
Waiting quietly to be rescued
Never sleeping on watch and signalling hard when a ship appears
Building a bigger raft
quiz.explanation: The castaway who keeps watching and signals determinedly when a sail appears is his model.

cards.title: Small courtesies exist to show regard for others
cards.body:
In a debate about 'the simple life', some readers scorned the petty rituals of modern life: greetings, small talk, social customs. Bennett defended them. Conventions in life are like form in art, he says. Too much is stifling, but without them life loses shape.

Above all, these customs are a quick, shared way of showing that you care about other people's feelings. Drop them and you don't gain authenticity; you mostly lose friends and inconvenience everyone. A greeting or a thank-you is cheap, and it says a lot.
cards.quote: I cannot too strongly insist that the basis of convention is a symbolism, primarily meant to display a regard for the feelings of other people.
cards.apply_it: Today, pick one courtesy you usually skip, like a proper greeting or a thank-you message, and do it deliberately.

quiz.question: Why does Bennett defend social conventions?
options: They are ancient traditions
They are required by law
They help you get ahead at work
They are a quick way to show regard for other people's feelings
quiz.explanation: He says the basis of convention is symbolism meant to show regard for others' feelings.

cards.title: You can't be in self-improvement mode all the time
cards.body:
Bennett warns that no one can stay at full strain on self-improvement every waking hour. Human nature won't stand it. Ordinary routines and pleasant small rituals fill time we'd otherwise be unable to use, and they give the striving part of us a rest.

He adds that people who did nothing but cultivate their noblest faculties would become insufferable prigs. A healthy life has room for growth and for ordinary, unimproving moments, and that balance makes the growth sustainable.
cards.quote: And the other reason is that one cannot always be at the full strain of ‘self-improvement,’ and ‘evolutionary progress,’ and generally beating the big drum. Human nature will not stand it.
cards.apply_it: Schedule one block this week for something purely enjoyable with no self-improvement goal attached.

quiz.question: What does Bennett say about striving to improve every waking hour?
options: Human nature can't sustain it
It's the only path to success
It's easy once you form the habit
It's what the greatest people did
quiz.explanation: He says one cannot always be at full strain on self-improvement; human nature won't stand it.

cards.title: Direct your mind; don't leave it to wander unattended
cards.body:
In his final essay, Bennett describes the source of his own contentment: the sense that he is in charge of his mind, rather than the other way round. He calls the mind an unruly servant that becomes less unruly with practice.

His method is regular meditation: deciding beforehand what the mind should dwell on and insisting it go there, rather than leaving it idle and directionless. He admits it is hard, but says it is very much worth doing, and that the lack of reflective habits was the great fault of his busy age, as it may be of ours.
cards.quote: also by never leaving it idle, undirected, masterless, to play at random like a child in the streets after dark.
cards.apply_it: Before a commute or walk, choose one thought or question to reflect on. Each time your mind drifts, guide it back.

quiz.question: How does Bennett say the mind can be brought under control?
options: By keeping it constantly entertained
By regular meditation and deciding in advance where it should go
By avoiding all difficult thoughts
By sleeping more
quiz.explanation: He recommends regular meditation and choosing beforehand what the mind should focus on.

cards.title: Calm and charity toward others are a steady path to contentment
cards.body:
Bennett ends the book with the two habits he believed brought him contentment. The first is calm: reminding himself daily that everyday accidents, a missed train or a setback, can't touch what is deepest in him. The second is charity: seeing every person as fundamentally like himself, which melts blame, irritation and resentment.

He admits there's nothing new in this. But he thought that letting go of the habit of judging and condemning others was essential to real peace, and that thinking deeply tends to make people happier, not sadder.
cards.quote: being fully convinced that in calmness and in charity lies the secret of a placid if not ecstatic happiness.
cards.apply_it: The next time someone irritates you, pause and think of one way they are like you. Notice what happens to the irritation.

quiz.question: Which two qualities does Bennett see as the secret of contentment?
options: Wealth and fame
Ambition and discipline
Calmness and charity
Solitude and silence
quiz.explanation: He concludes that in calmness and in charity lies the secret of a placid happiness.
